newsitem.title: JAPAN: CS Financial Products to enter Japanese market.
newsitem.headline: CS Financial Products to enter Japanese market.

text.p: Credit Suisse Financial Products (CSFP), a member of Credit Suisse First Boston Group specialized in risk management services, said on Monday that it will open its first overseas branch in Japan on Tuesday.

Christopher Goekjian, president and CEO of CSFP, told a news conference in Tokyo that his firm sees a particularly opportune time for starting operations in Japan, given the current Japanese economic circumstances and planned "Big Bang" financial deregulations.

"We believe that as these markets are deregulated, people will make more use of risk management products, and this is a big drive and one of the reasons why we are opening a branch in Japan," he said.

Credit Suisse Financial Products, a global derivative power house based in London, specializes in products such as interest rate swap and options, currency and equity swaps as well as risk management services.
Speaking at the same news conference, Tokyo Branch Manager Shinji Yamada said: "We expect further deregulation will promote the expansion of our profits in the future."
He added that the new branch office will have approximately 90 employees, half of whom will engage in developing risk management products.

The Japanese Ministry of Finance granted an official banking licence to CSFP in February. According to a Finance Ministry official, CSFP is the first foreign financial institution, specialising primarily in derivatives products and risk management services, to acquire the Japanese licence.
Under Japan's Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law, only licensed institutions can conduct foreign exchange business here.

Goekjian said Tokyo is looking more attractive for CSFP's products than other Asian financial markets while costs for conducting business in Tokyo are becoming less due to recent weakness in yen against the U.S. dollar.
He added that CSFP is setting up a subsidiary in Hong Kong to cover the Southeast Asian region in the next three months, although its operation will be smaller than the one in Tokyo.
